# AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents

Bohan Yu, Pengfei Cao, Kai Tian, Chen Han, Shi-Yang Li, Chenxi Zhou,
Junlin Liu, Cao Liu, Ke Zeng, Jun Zhao, Kang Liu²²footnotemark: 2 School
of Advanced Interdisciplinary Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of
Sciences The Key Laboratory of Cognition and Decision Intelligence for
Complex Systems, Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of
Sciences Meituan yubohan2025@ia.ac.cn
 {pengfei.cao,jzhao,kliu}@nlpr.ia.ac.cn ^(†)^(†)thanks:   Corresponding
authors.

###### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) possess broad factual knowledge and strong
reasoning capabilities, but solving complex tasks also requires
procedural knowledge about how to act. Existing approaches often
represent procedural knowledge through trajectories or bundled skills,
limiting flexible reuse across interaction histories. This paper
introduces Procedural Atoms, fine-grained and independently applicable
units that represent _Intent_, _When_, _Do_, and _Avoid_ guidance.
Building on this representation, we propose AtomSD, an Atom-guided
Self-Distillation framework in which the learner continually extracts
Procedural Atoms from its own successful trajectories and distills them
into the evolving policy through Atom-conditioned supervision and
task-reward optimization. Comprehensive experiments show that AtomSD
consistently outperforms strong reward-based and distillation methods,
exceeding the state-of-the-art baseline by up to 9.31 points in average
performance. Further analyses demonstrate that the proposed Procedural
Atoms provide effective guidance, highlighting the value of atom-level
procedural knowledge for policy learning. [
 GitHub](https://github.com/SharkSpicy-NLP/AtomSD)

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have acquired extensive factual knowledge
and strong reasoning capabilities, enabling them to tackle increasingly
complex tasks across diverse domains ([OpenAI et al., 2024](#bib.bib2);
[Zhao et al., 2026b](#bib.bib3)). However, knowing the relevant facts
does not necessarily imply knowing how to act. For example, a model may
understand the properties of every reagent in a scientific experiment,
yet still fail to execute the experimental procedure correctly. Such
failures reflect the difference between declarative knowledge about a
domain and procedural knowledge or planning knowledge about how tasks
within that domain should be carried out. It becomes particularly
consequential when successful behavior depends on sequences of
interdependent decisions rather than isolated answers. In such contexts,
an agent must determine which operations advance a goal, when their
prerequisites hold, how intermediate results constrain later actions,
and how its procedure should adapt as conditions change ([Shridhar et
al., 2021](#bib.bib13); [Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib14); [Yao et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib15); [Yu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib37)). Therefore, learning
reusable procedural knowledge is an important step toward translating
the broad capabilities of LLMs into reliable performance in complex
tasks.

Toward this goal, existing approaches leverage interaction trajectories
to construct and transfer reusable procedural knowledge, broadly
following two directions. (1) _Organizing trajectories into reusable
guidance_. Prior work transforms previous interactions into reflections,
workflows, skills, or conditional rules that can guide subsequent
behavior through prompting ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Mi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib33); [Liang et al., 2026](#bib.bib41); [Sun et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40)). Such representations abstract beyond individual
actions and make past experience accessible across future interactions.
(2) _Distilling experience into the policy_. A second line of work
transfers knowledge from demonstrations, feedback, or skill-augmented
teacher context into the learner itself, allowing the resulting policy
to benefit from this supervision without requiring the same external
guidance at inference time ([Zhao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib20); [Hübotter
et al., 2026](#bib.bib21); [Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib22); [Lu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23)).

![Refer to caption](2610.26926v1/pre.png)

Figure 1: Procedural Atoms enable fine-grained reuse and composition of
procedural knowledge.

Despite their effectiveness, these approaches leave two important
questions unresolved. (1) _What should be the reusable unit of
procedural knowledge?_ As shown in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents"),
complete trajectories retain instance-specific objects, observations,
and action sequences, while workflows and skills often bundle multiple
operations into a single unit of guidance. Both can limit transfer
across interaction histories: a new execution may require only a subset
of the operations in a previous procedure, or may need to compose
operations learned from different experiences. This calls for
finer-grained procedural units that can be independently reused and
flexibly composed across interaction histories. (2) _How should
procedural knowledge evolve with the learner?_ Existing approaches often
rely on separately maintained skill libraries or external models to
derive and update guidance from interaction trajectories ([Mi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib33); [Lu et al., 2026](#bib.bib23); [Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib22); [Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib12)). However, reusable
procedural knowledge should ideally co-evolve with the policy itself: as
the learner acquires new capabilities and succeeds on new interaction
histories, the knowledge available for subsequent learning should be
updated accordingly. In a word, the aforementioned limitations motivate
us to ask: _what form of procedural knowledge can be extracted from
previous interactions, and continuously distilled as the learner
evolves?_

To this end, this paper proposes AtomSD, a procedural Atom-guided
Self-Distillation framework that couples continual procedural
abstraction with online policy learning. To provide a reusable unit of
procedural knowledge, we define a _Procedural Atom_ as a fine-grained
and independently applicable unit of procedural knowledge. As
illustrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents"),
a Procedural Atom consists of (i) _Intent_, specifying what the
procedure is intended to accomplish; (ii) _When_, defining its
applicability conditions; (iii) _Do_, specifying an ordered procedure;
and (iv) _Avoid_, identifying operations or failure modes to avoid. With
this goal-directed and condition-aware representation, individual Atoms
can be selectively applied and flexibly composed across different
interaction histories, rather than reused only in complete and
inseparable trajectories or bundled workflows. In this way, procedural
knowledge can better adapt to new interactions.

To enable procedural knowledge to co-evolve with the learner, AtomSD
establishes a self-improving loop through two complementary processes.
(1) _Online procedural abstraction_. At each training iteration, the
student acts as its own knowledge extractor, abstracting successful
on-policy trajectories into independently applicable Procedural Atoms.
By sharing the resulting Atom set within the same task, knowledge
extracted from one trajectory can guide other interaction histories,
including both successful and failed ones. As the policy evolves,
subsequent extraction continually refreshes the procedural guidance to
reflect the learner’s growing capabilities. (2) _Atom-guided
self-distillation_. An Atom-conditioned teacher, derived from the
student, evaluates the original on-policy trajectories, transforming
self-extracted procedural knowledge into token-level supervision across
different interaction histories. Through joint reward optimization and
self-distillation, this guidance is progressively internalized into the
policy, whose continued improvement in turn supports further procedural
knowledge discovery.

Comprehensive experiments on widely used benchmarks ([Shridhar et al.,
2021](#bib.bib13); [Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib14); [Yao et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib15); [Guo et al., 2025b](#bib.bib16)) demonstrate that
AtomSD consistently outperforms six strong reward-based and distillation
baselines, while also showing competitive performance against advanced
API-based models such as DeepSeek-V4-Pro ([DeepSeek-AI et al.,
2026](#bib.bib1)) and GPT-5.5 ([OpenAI, 2026](#bib.bib25)). AtomSD
exceeds the state-of-the-art baseline in average performance by up to
9.31 points, with improvements extending to unseen tasks. Further
analyses show that fine-grained Procedural Atoms provide compact and
effective guidance, validating the design of Atom-guided
self-distillation.

Our key contributions are as follows:

- •
  This paper introduces Procedural Atoms, fine-grained and independently
  applicable units that support selective reuse and flexible composition
  of procedural knowledge across interaction histories.
- •
  AtomSD combines online procedural abstraction with Atom-guided
  self-distillation, allowing procedural knowledge to be progressively
  internalized into the policy while co-evolving with the learner.

## 2 Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation

As shown in
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents"),
this paper proposes _Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation_ as a
self-improving loop in which procedural knowledge is continually
extracted from on-policy interactions and internalized into the evolving
student policy. We define _Procedural Atoms_ as fine-grained functional
units of procedural knowledge that capture guidance across four aspects:
_Intent_, _When_, _Do_, and _Avoid_. As training proceeds iteratively,
the student policy is updated at each training iteration based on its
newly generated on-policy interactions. We formulate each training
iteration as one complete self-improving loop consisting of two coupled
processes: (1) _Online Procedural Abstraction_ and (2) _Atom-Guided
Self-Distillation_.

![Refer to caption](2610.26926v1/main.png)

Figure 2: Overview of AtomSD. Procedural Atoms are continually
abstracted from the student’s own successful trajectories and distilled
back into the evolving policy through Atom-guided self-distillation.

### 2.1 Online Procedural Abstraction

We represent an interaction trajectory $`\tau`$ as a task together with
the sequence of observations and actions encountered during execution.
From its own successful trajectories, the evolving student serves as the
procedural knowledge extractor, abstracting reusable procedures into
independently applicable Procedural Atoms.

#### Atom Structure

Formally, an Atom $`\omega`$ is represented as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\omega=\left\langle\iota_{\omega},\mathcal{C}_{\omega},\mathcal{P}_{\omega},\mathcal{B}_{\omega}\right\rangle,
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\iota_{\omega}`$ denotes the procedural intent;
$`\mathcal{C}_{\omega}=\{c_{\omega,1},\ldots,c_{\omega,n_{C}}\}`$
specifies the conditions under which the Atom applies;
$`\mathcal{P}_{\omega}=(p_{\omega,1},\ldots,p_{\omega,n_{P}})`$ defines
the ordered procedure to execute; and
$`\mathcal{B}_{\omega}=\{b_{\omega,1},\ldots,b_{\omega,n_{B}}\}`$
captures optional failure modes or inappropriate operations to avoid.
Here, the elements of $`\mathcal{C}_{\omega}`$,
$`\mathcal{P}_{\omega}`$, and $`\mathcal{B}_{\omega}`$ denote the
conditions, operations, and avoidance items, respectively, while
$`n_{C}`$, $`n_{P}`$, and $`n_{B}`$ denote their respective counts.
Together, these components characterize what to achieve, when to apply
the Atom, how to act, and what boundaries to respect.

Atom Example

The following example illustrates how a Procedural Atom $`\omega`$
instantiates the four components defined above.

Intent $`(\iota_{\omega})`$: Clean a held object using a designated
cleaning facility. When $`(\mathcal{C}_{\omega})`$: The agent holds an
object requiring cleaning; a suitable cleaning facility is available. Do
$`(\mathcal{P}_{\omega})`$: Navigate to the cleaning facility if not
already there; execute the cleaning action with the held object and the
facility. Avoid $`(\mathcal{B}_{\omega})`$: Attempting to clean without
reaching the facility; cleaning an object that is not currently held;
using an incorrect or unavailable cleaning method.

#### Atomization and Sharing

To provide fine-grained procedural knowledge for reuse across
interaction histories, we atomize successful trajectories and aggregate
their Atoms at the task level. Consider the $`k`$-th self-improving
iteration and a sampled task $`x`$ in its training batch. Let
$`\theta_{k}`$ denote the student parameters at the beginning of
iteration $`k`$. For task $`x`$, the current student
$`\pi_{\theta_{k}}`$ generates $`G`$ on-policy trajectories
$`\mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}=\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$ without access to
Procedural Atoms. Within $`\mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}`$, we identify the
successful trajectories as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{S}_{x}^{(k)}=\{\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}\mid s(\tau_{i})=1\},
``` |  | (2) |

where $`s(\tau_{i})\in\{0,1\}`$ indicates whether $`\tau_{i}`$
successfully completes task $`x`$. The current student then serves as
its own procedural knowledge extractor, atomizing each successful
trajectory $`\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{x}^{(k)}`$ using the extraction
prompt shown in
Figure [8](#A4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Internalization and Composition ‣ D.2 Composition of Internalized Atoms ‣ Appendix D Qualitative Case Studies ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents"):

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{i}^{(k)}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\textsc{Extract}\bigl(\pi_{\theta_{k}};\tau_{i}\bigr)=\left\{\omega_{i,r}=\left\langle\iota_{\omega_{i,r}},\mathcal{C}_{\omega_{i,r}},\mathcal{P}_{\omega_{i,r}},\mathcal{B}_{\omega_{i,r}}\right\rangle\right\}_{r=1}^{M_{i}},`$ |  | (3) |

where $`M_{i}`$ denotes the number of Procedural Atoms extracted from
$`\tau_{i}`$. The trajectory-level Atom sets are then aggregated into
the task-level procedural knowledge of the current self-improving loop:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Omega_{x}^{(k)}=\bigcup_{\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{x}^{(k)}}\mathcal{A}_{i}^{(k)}.
``` |  | (4) |

1: Initial student policy $`\pi_{\theta_{0}}`$; task distribution
$`\mathcal{D}`$; number of on-policy trajectories per task $`G`$;
distillation weight $`\lambda`$; clipping range $`\epsilon`$; EMA decay
$`\alpha`$; training iterations $`K`$

2: Trained student policy $`\pi_{\theta_{K}}`$

3: Initialize teacher parameters $`\phi_{0}\leftarrow\theta_{0}`$

4: for $`k\leftarrow 0`$ to $`K-1`$ do

5:   Sample a training batch $`\mathcal{X}^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{D}`$

6:   for all $`x\in\mathcal{X}^{(k)}`$ do

7: (1) Online Procedural Abstraction

8:    Generate
$`\mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}=\{\tau_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid x)\}_{i=1}^{G}`$

9:
   $`\mathcal{S}_{x}^{(k)}\leftarrow\{\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}\mid s(\tau_{i})=1\}`$
$`\triangleright`$ successful trajectories

10:
   $`\mathcal{A}_{i}^{(k)}\leftarrow\textsc{Extract}(\pi_{\theta_{k}};\tau_{i})=\{\omega_{i,r}\}_{r=1}^{M_{i}}`$,
$`\forall\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{x}^{(k)}`$

11:
   $`\Omega_{x}^{(k)}\leftarrow\displaystyle\bigcup_{\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{x}^{(k)}}\mathcal{A}_{i}^{(k)}`$
$`\triangleright`$ task-level Atom set

12: (2) Atom-Guided Self-Distillation

13:    Compute $`A_{i}^{\mathrm{RL},(k)}`$ for all
$`\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}`$ $`\triangleright`$ reward signal

14:
   $`q_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)}\leftarrow\pi_{\phi_{k}}(y_{ij}\mid h_{ij},\Omega_{x}^{(k)})`$
$`\triangleright`$ Atom support

15:    Compute $`A_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)}`$ from
$`q_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)}`$ using
Eq. ([6](#S2.E6 "In Joint Optimization ‣ 2.2 Atom-Guided Self-Distillation ‣ 2 Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents"))

16:   end for

17:   $`\theta_{k+1}\leftarrow\textsc{Update}(\theta_{k})`$ using all
$`A_{i}^{\mathrm{RL},(k)}`$ and $`A_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)}`$ over
$`\mathcal{X}^{(k)}`$ via
Eq. ([8](#S2.E8 "In Joint Optimization ‣ 2.2 Atom-Guided Self-Distillation ‣ 2 Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents"))
with $`\lambda`$ and $`\epsilon`$ $`\triangleright`$ policy update

18:   $`\phi_{k+1}\leftarrow\alpha\phi_{k}+(1-\alpha)\theta_{k+1}`$
$`\triangleright`$ EMA teacher update

19: end for

20: return $`\pi_{\theta_{K}}`$

Algorithm 1 AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation

The resulting $`\Omega_{x}^{(k)}`$ aggregates procedural knowledge
discovered across successful trajectories while retaining the
constituent Atoms as distinct units. It is then shared across all
trajectories of task $`x`$ to provide reusable guidance over different
interaction histories, including both successful and unsuccessful ones.

### 2.2 Atom-Guided Self-Distillation

The second process completes each self-improving loop by distilling the
procedural knowledge $`\Omega_{x}^{(k)}`$ extracted from the current
student back into its policy. Conditioned on this shared Atom set, the
teacher provides token-level procedural supervision over the student’s
on-policy interaction histories.
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Atomization and Sharing ‣ 2.1 Online Procedural Abstraction ‣ 2 Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
summarizes the complete self-improving loop executed at each training
iteration.

#### Atom-Conditioned Guidance

Let $`\phi_{k}`$ denote the teacher parameters at iteration $`k`$. For
each trajectory $`\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}`$ and the $`j`$-th
student-generated token $`y_{ij}`$ in $`\tau_{i}`$, let $`h_{ij}`$
denote its preceding token-level interaction history. Given the shared
task-level Atom set $`\Omega_{x}^{(k)}`$ and the teacher prompting
template shown in
Figure [9](#A4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Internalization and Composition ‣ D.2 Composition of Internalized Atoms ‣ Appendix D Qualitative Case Studies ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents"),
the teacher’s Atom-conditioned token-level support for $`y_{ij}`$ is
defined as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)}=\pi_{\phi_{k}}\left(y_{ij}\mid h_{ij},\Omega_{x}^{(k)}\right).
``` |  | (5) |

For each Atom $`\omega\in\Omega_{x}^{(k)}`$, the intent
$`\iota_{\omega}`$ and applicability conditions $`\mathcal{C}_{\omega}`$
provide the basis for identifying relevant Atoms from the current
history $`h_{ij}`$, while $`\mathcal{P}_{\omega}`$ and
$`\mathcal{B}_{\omega}`$ provide the corresponding procedural guidance
and boundaries. Conditioning jointly on $`h_{ij}`$ and
$`\Omega_{x}^{(k)}`$ allows the teacher to draw on relevant Atom
guidance while providing history-specific token-level supervision,
enabling compositional procedural guidance across multiple Atoms.

#### Joint Optimization

We convert the Atom-conditioned support from a teacher derived from the
student into a token-level internalization signal:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle A_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname{sg}\!\left[\log q_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)}-\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{ij}\mid h_{ij})\right],`$ |  | (6) |

where $`\operatorname{sg}(\cdot)`$ denotes stop-gradient. This signal
captures the difference between the teacher’s support under the
extracted procedural knowledge and the student’s corresponding unguided
probability.

In parallel, environment feedback provides a trajectory-level learning
signal. For the $`G`$ trajectories in $`\mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}`$, we
compute the GRPO advantage ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)) as
$`A_{i}^{\mathrm{RL},(k)}=(R(\tau_{i})-\overline{R}_{x}^{(k)})/\sigma_{x}^{(k)}`$,
where $`\overline{R}_{x}^{(k)}`$ and $`\sigma_{x}^{(k)}`$ denote the
within-task reward mean and standard deviation. The policy ratio is
$`r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(y_{ij}\mid h_{ij})/\pi_{\theta_{k}}(y_{ij}\mid h_{ij})`$.
Both learning signals use the same PPO-style clipped surrogate
loss ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib29)):

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\ell_{\mathrm{clip}}\!\left(r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta),A\right)`$ | $`\displaystyle=-\min\Bigl\{r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta)A,\operatorname{clip}\!\left(r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)A\Bigr\},`$ |  | (7) |

where $`\operatorname{clip}(\cdot)`$ constrains the policy ratio to
$`[1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon]`$, and $`A`$ denotes the corresponding reward
or Atom-guided distillation signal. Combining the two signals, the
task-level objective is

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{x}^{(k)}(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{G}L_{i}}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{i}}\Big[\ell_{\mathrm{clip}}\!\left(r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta),A_{i}^{\mathrm{RL},(k)}\right)+\lambda\,\ell_{\mathrm{clip}}\!\left(r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta),A_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)}\right)\Big],`$ |  | (8) |

where $`L_{i}`$ counts valid student-generated tokens in $`\tau_{i}`$,
and $`\lambda`$ controls the strength of distillation. The batch
objective aggregates these task-level losses according to their valid
token counts. Optimizing this objective updates the student from
$`\pi_{\theta_{k}}`$ to $`\pi_{\theta_{k+1}}`$, progressively
internalizing the procedural knowledge represented by
$`\Omega_{x}^{(k)}`$ into the policy.

#### Teacher Update

The teacher and student are initialized identically,
$`\phi_{0}=\theta_{0}`$. After optimizing each training iteration, the
teacher is updated by exponential moving average (EMA):

|     |                                                   |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \phi_{k+1}=\alpha\phi_{k}+(1-\alpha)\theta_{k+1},
       ```                                                |     | (9) |

where $`\alpha`$ denotes the EMA decay. The updated student
$`\pi_{\theta_{k+1}}`$ then serves as the basis for procedural
abstraction in the next iteration. Repeating this loop continually
externalizes procedural knowledge from the evolving learner and distills
it back into the policy, allowing procedural knowledge and the policy to
co-evolve throughout training.

## 3 Experiments

### 3.1 Experiment Settings

#### Benchmarks

We evaluate agents’ ability to follow and execute multi-step procedures
across four benchmarks. ALFWorld (ALF) ([Shridhar et al.,
2021](#bib.bib13)) assesses household planning and execution in
text-based environments. ScienceWorld (SW) ([Wang et al.,
2022](#bib.bib14)) requires scientific reasoning through multi-step
experimentation. WebShop (WS) ([Yao et al., 2023a](#bib.bib15))
evaluates product search and purchasing under user constraints.
StableToolBench (STB) ([Guo et al., 2025b](#bib.bib16)) assesses tool
use through a virtual API environment. We report seen and unseen results
separately for ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, denoted by the suffixes -S and
-U, alongside test results for WebShop and StableToolBench. Detailed
descriptions of the datasets and evaluation subsets are provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Datasets ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents").

#### Models

We use Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib17)) as
backbone models. We additionally evaluate four strong API-based models:
DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro ([DeepSeek-AI et al.,
2026](#bib.bib1)), GLM-5.3 ([GLM-5-Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)), and
GPT-5.5 ([OpenAI, 2026](#bib.bib25)).

#### Baselines

All models interact with the environments using ReAct ([Yao et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib18)). API-based models are evaluated with ReAct alone. We
compare AtomSD with the following categories of methods: (1) Prompting:
the initial model with ReAct alone and Reflexion ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib30)), which additionally incorporates textual reflections
from previous attempts without parameter updates; (2) Reward-based RL:
GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)), which learns from task rewards;
(3) Trajectory-guided self-distillation: OPSD ([Zhao et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib20)), SDPO ([Hübotter et al., 2026](#bib.bib21)), and
GRPO+OPSD, which use successful demonstrations as privileged teacher
context in our setting, with GRPO+OPSD additionally incorporating task
rewards; and (4) Skill-guided distillation: Skill-SD ([Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib22)) and SDAR ([Lu et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)), which
combine reward optimization with teacher guidance from skills
constructed by strong external LLMs. Together, these baselines provide a
comprehensive comparison across inference-time reflection, reward-based
learning, and trajectory- or skill-guided distillation. We set
$`\lambda=0.001`$, $`\alpha=0.95`$, and $`\epsilon=0.2`$ for AtomSD.
Detailed training and implementation settings are provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Training and Implementation Details ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents").

#### Evaluation Metrics

For training-based methods, we evaluate checkpoints at the same training
step. We report success rate on ALFWorld, average task score on
ScienceWorld and WebShop, and solved rate on StableToolBench using the
official Final Answer Completeness (FAC) ([Guo et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib42)). All scores use a 0–100 scale.

### 3.2 Main Results

Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Teacher Update ‣ 2.2 Atom-Guided Self-Distillation ‣ 2 Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
summarizes the main results, with four key findings. (1) AtomSD improves
beyond reward- and demonstration-guided training. AtomSD consistently
outperforms GRPO, OPSD, and GRPO+OPSD in average performance at both
model scales, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.31 and 5.42 points
at 4B and 9B, respectively. This highlights the value of Procedural
Atoms beyond reward-only learning, demonstration-guided distillation,
and their combination. (2) AtomSD provides broader gains than
skill-level distillation. AtomSD outperforms Skill-SD and SDAR on most
tasks at both scales, with particularly pronounced gains on
ScienceWorld. These results suggest that even skill libraries
constructed by stronger external models do not necessarily provide more
effective guidance, highlighting the value of fine-grained Procedural
Atoms. (3) Improvements generalize to unseen tasks. AtomSD leads on
ScienceWorld unseen at both model scales, with improvements also
extending to ALFWorld unseen. These results suggest that procedural
knowledge learned through AtomSD can generalize beyond seen tasks. (4)
AtomSD is competitive with strong LLMs without inference-time
reflection. AtomSD surpasses Reflexion by 22.91 and 20.85 points at 4B
and 9B, respectively. AtomSD-9B further exceeds DeepSeek-V4-Pro and
trails GPT-5.5 by only 5.39 points in average score, suggesting that
internalizing Procedural Atom guidance can reduce reliance on
inference-time reflection while narrowing the gap to substantially
stronger LLMs. We further provide qualitative case studies in
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Procedural Dependency Patterns ‣ Appendix D Qualitative Case Studies ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents").

### 3.3 Effects of Atom Components and Joint Optimization

Figure [3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Table 1 ‣ Teacher Update ‣ 2.2 Atom-Guided Self-Distillation ‣ 2 Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
examines the contributions of Atom components and joint reward
optimization. (1) The complete Atom representation provides more
effective guidance. Including Intent improves the average score by 15.0
points at 4B and 1.4 points at 9B, while the complete representation
outperforms removing both Intent and Avoid by 8.9 and 13.4 points,
respectively, with similar trends observed in the training rewards.
These results highlight the value of organizing procedural guidance
within the complete Atom representation. (2) Explicit avoidance
boundaries improve performance at both scales. Removing Avoid reduces
the average score by 13.1 points at 4B and 14.0 points at 9B. This
further highlights the importance of explicitly representing what to
avoid, rather than distilling successful operations alone. (3) Joint
optimization strengthens Atom-guided learning. Combining Atom-guided
distillation with task rewards improves average performance by 25.3 and
25.1 points over Atom-only training at 4B and 9B, respectively. This
supports the design choice of jointly internalizing procedural guidance
while optimizing for task completion. Overall, these results show that
effective Atom-guided learning depends on both a complete procedural
representation and joint optimization with task rewards.

across Early/Late training and same-/cross-task histories, reporting

### 3.4 Internalization and Co-Evolution

#### Internalization and Composition

To examine whether the student internalizes Atom guidance, we consider
two relevant Procedural Atoms, $`\omega_{\alpha}`$ and
$`\omega_{\beta}`$, and evaluate guidance from each individually and in
combination. We use GPT-5.5 to identify supported actions and their
preceding interaction histories. This analysis covers both same-task and
cross-task histories at two training stages, Early and Late. Within each
stage, we use a fixed training interval and compare the student
checkpoints at its beginning and end using two metrics: (1)
*maximum-token support change*, measuring the relative probability
increase of the most-improved action token without Atoms, and (2)
*guidance-direction agreement*, measuring whether Atom-favored tokens
change in the same direction after training without Atoms. Detailed
definitions and results are provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Procedural Atom Internalization and Composition Analysis ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents").
As shown in
Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 Effects of Atom Components and Joint Optimization ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents"),
during Early training, maximum-token support ($`\Delta p/p`$) increases
by 36.9% for 4B and 45.2% for 9B on same-task histories. Agreement with
composed guidance from $`\omega_{\alpha}`$ and $`\omega_{\beta}`$
reaches 75.0% on cross-task histories for Early 4B and 70.5% for Late
9B. These results support effective internalization of both individual
and composed Atom guidance, including across tasks; see
Appendix [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Composition of Internalized Atoms ‣ Appendix D Qualitative Case Studies ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
for a concrete composition case.

#### Co-Evolution

To assess whether procedural knowledge benefits from co-evolving with
the learner, we replace the evolving student extractor with either
DeepSeek-V4-Pro or the frozen initial Qwen backbone.
Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 Effects of Atom Components and Joint Optimization ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
(top) shows that a stronger extractor alone does not yield better
performance: DeepSeek-V4-Pro trails AtomSD at 4B and is comparable at
9B. Meanwhile, the evolving student consistently outperforms the frozen
extractor in evaluation performance and late-stage rewards at both
scales. These results support AtomSD’s co-evolving design: learner
improvement refreshes procedural knowledge for distillation, which in
turn supports further policy improvement.

#### Atom Representation

To characterize the granularity and compactness of Procedural Atoms,
Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 Effects of Atom Components and Joint Optimization ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
(bottom left) compares lengths using trajectories matched by task and
training step across methods. Overall, Atom guidance requires 1.53k
prefix tokens, compared with 2.20k for skills and 3.93k for
trajectories. At the unit level, individual Atoms average only 0.15k
tokens, substantially smaller than skills (0.64k) and trajectories
(4.97k).
Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 Effects of Atom Components and Joint Optimization ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
(bottom right) further shows a relatively balanced distribution of the
four Atom components across datasets throughout training. These results
show that Procedural Atoms provide compact, fine-grained guidance across
multiple procedural aspects, supporting selective reuse and composition.

### 3.5 Analyses

#### Training Dynamics Analysis

Figure [7](#S3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Atom Representation ‣ 3.4 Internalization and Co-Evolution ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
(top) shows that AtomSD’s advantage emerges as training progresses. OPSD
improves rapidly early on at both model scales, but its gains
subsequently plateau, whereas AtomSD continues to improve and reaches
the highest reward toward the end.
Figure [7](#S3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Atom Representation ‣ 3.4 Internalization and Co-Evolution ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
(bottom) further shows that these gains accompany relatively low token
usage and fewer interaction steps during later training at both scales.
These results show that Procedural Atoms improve performance with more
compact trajectories.

#### Distillation Strength Analysis

Figure [7](#S3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Atom Representation ‣ 3.4 Internalization and Co-Evolution ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
shows that increasing $`\lambda`$ from 0.001 to 0.01 or 0.1 consistently
reduces late-stage training rewards and average evaluation performance
at both model scales. This suggests that Atom-guided distillation is
more effective when properly balanced with reward optimization rather
than simply strengthened, consistent with recent findings on
self-distillation in agentic RL ([Lu et al., 2026](#bib.bib23); [Kaur et
al., 2026](#bib.bib39)).

#### Teacher Update Analysis

Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 Effects of Atom Components and Joint Optimization ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
(middle) compares EMA with fixed and fully synchronized teachers. EMA
achieves the highest average evaluation performance at both model
scales; the fixed teacher remains competitive, while full
synchronization yields lower late-stage training rewards at both scales.
These results suggest that EMA balances preserving prior teacher
knowledge with incorporating student progress.

## 4 Related Work

#### Experiential Memory and Procedural Knowledge

Experience-based agents transform interaction histories into
reflections, insights, and reasoning memories for reuse in subsequent
decisions ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib30); [Zhao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib6); [Ouyang et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)), while others
leverage embeddings, KV cache, or special tokens to represent
memories ([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib43); [Yu et al., 2026c](#bib.bib44);
[Wu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib45)). Furthermore, prior work organizes
histories into reusable workflows, conditional procedures, and explicit
rules, enabling more selective reuse across interactions ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib31); [Fu et al., 2024](#bib.bib32); [Lin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib9); [Yu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Mi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib33)). A complementary line of work models environment
dynamics and action consequences to support planning ([Qiao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib26); [Kim and Hwang, 2025](#bib.bib27); [Liu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib28)). AtomSD instead uses procedural abstractions as
privileged context. Condition-aware Atoms guide policy learning and are
progressively internalized into model parameters, without requiring
external guidance at inference.

#### On-Policy Distillation

On-policy distillation applies teacher supervision to student-generated
trajectories, internalizing privileged knowledge into model
parameters ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib34); [Zhao et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib20); [Hübotter et al., 2026](#bib.bib21); [Ye et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10); [Wu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib47)). Privileged knowledge
can be supplied as explicit textual context or encoded into learned
latent representations ([Liu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib46); [Ye et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10); [Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)). AtomSD uses
independently applicable Procedural Atoms as the unit of privileged
supervision, enabling guidance to be composed according to the student’s
current interaction history rather than being tied to a specific
demonstration trajectory or workflow.

#### Skill-Guided Agent Learning

Skill-augmented reinforcement learning optimizes agents’ ability to
exploit and improve external skill libraries ([Wang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib35); [Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib8); [Chen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib49)). Skill-conditioned distillation instead uses skill
guidance as teacher-side context to train policies that operate without
external skill inputs at inference ([Lu et al., 2026](#bib.bib23); [Wang
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib22); [Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib12); [Lv et al.,
2026](#bib.bib48)). AtomSD constructs procedural guidance online from
the evolving student’s successful trajectories, without relying on a
preconstructed skill library or a separate external model for knowledge
extraction. By continually decomposing trajectories into independently
applicable Atoms rather than bundled skills, it supports selective reuse
and flexible composition while allowing procedural knowledge to
co-evolve with the learner.

## 5 Conclusion

This paper presents AtomSD, a self-improving framework that transforms
successful on-policy trajectories into Procedural Atoms and distills
their guidance back into the policy, allowing procedural knowledge to
co-evolve with the learner. Comprehensive experiments and analyses show
that AtomSD consistently improves agent performance, while fine-grained
Procedural Atoms support selective reuse and flexible composition across
interaction histories. Our results highlight atomized procedural
knowledge as an effective bridge between raw interaction histories and
parametric policy learning.

## Appendix A Datasets

We evaluate AtomSD on four agent benchmarks covering household
interaction, scientific experimentation, web shopping, and tool use.
These benchmarks differ substantially in task structure and interaction
requirements, providing a diverse testbed for procedural knowledge
learning.
Table [2](#A1.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Appendix A Datasets ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
summarizes their task characteristics, task diversity, and the number of
task instances available for training and used for evaluation.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  Benchmark | Task characteristics |  Task types |  Training |  Evaluation |
|  ALFWorld |  Household interaction with object search, navigation, and prerequisite-aware manipulation |  6 families |  3,553 |  140 seen / 134 unseen |
|  ScienceWorld |  Multi-step scientific experimentation involving transformations, measurement, circuits, and biological reasoning |  30 types |  3,592 |  194 seen / 211 unseen |
|  WebShop |  Interactive product search, attribute matching, option selection, and purchase |  Open-ended |  10,587 |  200 test |
|  StableToolBench |  Multi-turn tool use involving API selection, parameterization, and execution |  3 groups |  10,129 |  169 solvable |
|  Total |  |  |  27,861 |  1,048 |

Table 2: Dataset characteristics and task counts used for training and
evaluation.

#### ALFWorld

ALFWorld ([Shridhar et al., 2021](#bib.bib13)) evaluates text-based
household interaction across six task families: placing objects, placing
two objects, cleaning, heating, cooling, and examining an object under a
light. The benchmark requires agents to locate relevant objects, satisfy
action prerequisites, and execute multi-step plans. We use 3,553
training tasks and report results on 140 seen and 134 unseen evaluation
tasks.

#### ScienceWorld

ScienceWorld ([Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib14)) evaluates scientific
reasoning and experimentation across 30 task types, including material
transformations, electrical circuits, measurement, and biological
processes. We use 3,592 training tasks and evaluate on 194 seen and 211
unseen tasks.

#### WebShop

WebShop ([Yao et al., 2023a](#bib.bib15)) evaluates interactive shopping
agents that must search a product catalog, inspect product attributes
and options, and select an item satisfying a natural-language request.
Its diversity arises from open-ended product constraints and shopping
goals. We use 10,587 training tasks and 200 test tasks for evaluation.

#### StableToolBench

StableToolBench ([Guo et al., 2025b](#bib.bib16)) evaluates multi-turn
tool use across the G1, G2, and G3 query groups, requiring agents to
select appropriate APIs, construct valid calls, and reason over tool
responses. Our training pool contains 10,129 audited ToolBench ([Qin et
al., 2024](#bib.bib38)) queries, and evaluation uses the 169 solvable
instances in the StableToolBench reporting subset.

#### Evaluation Subsets

We use fixed evaluation subsets across all methods: 140 seen and 134
unseen tasks for ALFWorld, 194 seen and 211 unseen tasks for
ScienceWorld, 200 test tasks for WebShop, and 169 solvable queries for
StableToolBench. The ScienceWorld and WebShop subsets follow the
manifests released with ETO ([Song et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)), and the
same task selections are used for every method.

## Appendix B Training and Implementation Details

#### Shared Setup

We train AtomSD and all training baselines under a unified
mixed-benchmark setting using verl ([Sheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib36)) on
$`8\times`$ A100 80 GB GPUs, with tasks sampled from the training pools
of ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, and StableToolBench. At each
training iteration, we sample 48 tasks, with 12 drawn from each
benchmark, and generate four on-policy trajectories per task. Sampling
is balanced across task types for ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and
StableToolBench, while WebShop is sampled from a single task pool.
Training rewards are normalized to $`[0,1]`$: ALFWorld and
StableToolBench use binary success rewards, while ScienceWorld and
WebShop retain their graded rewards after scaling by 100. We use a
learning rate of $`1\times 10^{-6}`$; other shared training
hyperparameters are summarized in
Table [3](#A2.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Shared Setup ‣ Appendix B Training and Implementation Details ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents").
For AtomSD, we set the distillation coefficient to $`\lambda=0.001`$,
the clipping range to $`\epsilon=0.2`$, and the EMA decay to
$`\alpha=0.95`$, updating the teacher once per training iteration. All
training baselines follow the same shared setup, with method-specific
objectives, guidance sources, and teacher-update strategies summarized
in
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Inference-Only Baselines ‣ Appendix B Training and Implementation Details ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents").
For evaluation inference and Atom extraction, we set the temperature to
0.7 for Qwen3.5 models and 1.0 for API-based models. We disable thinking
wherever supported; for GLM-5.3, which requires thinking, we set the
reasoning effort to low.

|                              |                              |
|------------------------------|------------------------------|
| Parameter                    | Setting                      |
| Shared training settings     |                              |
|  Backbones                   |  Qwen3.5-4B / Qwen3.5-9B     |
|  Tasks per iteration         |  48 (12 per benchmark)       |
|  Rollouts per task           |  4                           |
|  Optimization mini-batch     |  12 tasks / 48 trajectories  |
|  Optimization epochs         |  1                           |
|  Learning rate               |  $`1\times 10^{-6}`$         |
|  Maximum context length      |  49,152 tokens               |
|  Rollout temperature         |  1.0                         |
|  Random seed                 |  42                          |
| AtomSD-specific settings     |                              |
|  KD coefficient $`\lambda`$  |  0.001                       |
|  EMA decay $`\alpha`$        |  0.95                        |
|  Teacher update              |  Every training iteration    |

Table 3: Shared training hyperparameters and AtomSD-specific settings.

#### Demonstration-Based Distillation

We follow the official teacher-update settings for the
demonstration-based baselines: OPSD and GRPO+OPSD use a teacher fixed at
the initial backbone, while SDPO maintains an EMA teacher.
Demonstrations are drawn from successful same-task rollouts in the
current batch, excluding the target trajectory.

#### Skill-Based Distillation

We reproduce Skill-SD and SDAR following the official implementation and
experimental settings released with SDAR, including their respective
teacher-update and distillation configurations. Both methods use a skill
library as privileged teacher context, while the student receives no
skill input. Skill-SD uses a distillation coefficient of 0.001, whereas
SDAR uses 0.01 with its original gating mechanism; both teachers use the
current student parameters at each training iteration. For ALFWorld and
WebShop, we use the skill libraries released with SDAR. For ScienceWorld
and StableToolBench, where corresponding libraries are unavailable, we
construct them following SDAR’s official setting, using the
SkillRL ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)) procedure with training-task
rollouts and GPT-5.5 as the library builder.

#### Inference-Only Baselines

ReAct performs a single episode per task without parameter updates.
Reflexion allows up to three attempts per task with task-local
reflection memory, stopping early upon success. We adapt the official
reflection prompt to all four benchmarks.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  Method |  GRPO reward loss |  Distillation weight |  Teacher update |  Distillation configuration |
|  GRPO |  Yes |  — |  — |  Task-reward optimization only. |
|  OPSD |  No |  1.0 |  Fixed |  Sampled-token reverse-KL surrogate with successful same-task demonstrations. |
|  GRPO+OPSD |  Yes |  0.001 |  Fixed |  Same demonstration-conditioned distillation objective as OPSD. |
|  SDPO |  No |  1.0 |  EMA ($`\alpha=0.95`$) |  Distribution-level self-distillation over the top-$`K`$ tokens and the aggregated tail probability, with $`K=100`$. |
|  Skill-SD |  Yes |  0.001 |  Full synchronization |  Differentiable importance-weighted $`k_{3}`$ divergence. |
|  SDAR |  Yes |  0.01 |  Full synchronization |  Detached sigmoid gating with $`\beta=5.0`$. |

Table 4: Method-specific configurations for the training baselines.

## Appendix C Procedural Atom Internalization and Composition Analysis

We define *procedural Atom internalization* as the transfer of explicit
Atom guidance into the student’s own policy, such that the same guidance
is reflected in its behavior even when Atoms are no longer provided. We
further examine whether this internalization extends to composed
guidance from multiple Atoms. To examine this process, we hold the
interaction history fixed and compare two sources of action-support
change: the change induced by explicitly supplying Atoms to an earlier
checkpoint, and the change produced by subsequent training without Atom
access. We quantify their relationship using two complementary metrics:
(1) *maximum-token support change*, which captures the strongest local
increase in support for an action, and (2) *guidance-direction
agreement*, which measures whether training-induced changes follow the
direction specified by explicit Atom guidance. We evaluate both
individual and composed Atom guidance across same-task and cross-task
histories at Early and Late stages of training.

#### Analysis Units

Each analysis unit consists of an interaction history, a recorded
action, and an Atom pair $`(\omega_{\alpha},\omega_{\beta})`$. We obtain
Atoms from successful training trajectories and use GPT-5.5 to assess
their applicability to the target history and identify procedural
dependencies or joint constraints relevant to the recorded action. For
same-task analysis, the target history comes from a different trajectory
of the same task, whereas for cross-task analysis, it comes from a task
with a distinct task ID. The 4B analysis includes 175 same-task and 144
cross-task units, while the 9B analysis includes 173 and 149 units,
respectively. We define Early as training steps 0–10 and Late as steps
50–60.

#### Conditional Action Support

Let $`u`$ index an analysis unit, let $`y_{uj}`$ denote the token at
position $`j`$ of its recorded action, and let $`\mathcal{J}_{u}`$
denote the positions of the scored action-content tokens. For each Atom
context
$`\Omega\in\{\varnothing,\{\omega_{\alpha}\},\{\omega_{\beta}\},\{\omega_{\alpha},\omega_{\beta}\}\}`$,
we teacher-force the recorded action and compute the token-level
log-probability

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ell_{\theta,uj}(\Omega)=\log\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{uj}\mid\widetilde{h}_{uj},\Omega\bigr),\qquad j\in\mathcal{J}_{u},
``` |  | (10) |

where $`\widetilde{h}_{uj}`$ contains the preceding interaction history
and the recorded action prefix before token $`j`$. We score only
action-content tokens, yielding their conditional support under each
Atom context.

#### Metric 1: Maximum-Token Support Change

Let $`\theta^{-}`$ and $`\theta^{+}`$ denote the earlier and later
checkpoints within an analysis interval. Without providing Atoms, we
define the training-induced log-probability change for each action token
as
$`d_{uj}=\ell_{\theta^{+},uj}(\varnothing)-\ell_{\theta^{-},uj}(\varnothing)`$.
For each analysis unit, we select the most-improved token:

|     |                                                               |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       j_{u}^{\mathrm{update}}=\arg\max_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{u}}d_{uj},
       ```                                                            |     | (11) |

with ties resolved by the earliest position. Its relative probability
change is $`r_{u}=\exp(d_{uj_{u}^{\mathrm{update}}})-1`$. For a set
$`\mathcal{U}`$ of analysis units, we report

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
S_{\mathrm{max}}=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{U}|}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}r_{u}.
``` |  | (12) |

$`S_{\mathrm{max}}`$ therefore measures the mean relative change in the
most-improved token of each recorded action.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Model | Stage | Hist. | $`N`$ | $`S_{\mathrm{max}}`$ (%) | $`D_{\alpha}`$ (%) | $`D_{\beta}`$ (%) | $`D_{\alpha\beta}`$ (%) |
| 4B | Early | Same | 175 | 36.9 | 68.4 | 64.9 | 67.4 |
|  |  | Cross | 144 | 16.9 | 70.8 | 72.9 | 75.0 |
|  | Late | Same | 175 | 21.2 | 52.7 | 50.0 | 56.3 |
|  |  | Cross | 144 | 5.8 | 47.1 | 46.1 | 44.2 |
| 9B | Early | Same | 173 | 45.2 | 59.0 | 56.0 | 54.4 |
|  |  | Cross | 149 | 25.9 | 69.9 | 68.7 | 61.9 |
|  | Late | Same | 173 | 38.1 | 70.5 | 61.0 | 69.0 |
|  |  | Cross | 149 | 8.1 | 75.8 | 70.3 | 70.5 |

Table 5: Procedural Atom internalization across model scales, training
stages, and history settings. $`N`$ denotes the number of analysis
units; $`S_{\mathrm{max}}`$ measures maximum-token support change;
$`D_{\alpha}`$, $`D_{\beta}`$, and $`D_{\alpha\beta}`$ measure
guidance-direction agreement for Atom $`\omega_{\alpha}`$, Atom
$`\omega_{\beta}`$, and their composition, respectively.

#### Metric 2: Guidance-Direction Agreement

For each nonempty Atom context $`\Omega`$, we measure its explicit
guidance effect at the earlier checkpoint as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{uj}^{\Omega}=\ell_{\theta^{-},uj}(\Omega)-\ell_{\theta^{-},uj}(\varnothing).
``` |  | (13) |

We then select the token with the largest guidance effect,
$`j_{u}^{\Omega}=\arg\max_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{u}}g_{uj}^{\Omega}`$,
independently for Atom $`\omega_{\alpha}`$, Atom $`\omega_{\beta}`$, and
their combination. This selection depends only on the earlier checkpoint
and is therefore independent of subsequent training changes. At the
selected token, we define directional agreement as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
c_{u}^{\Omega}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[g_{uj_{u}^{\Omega}}^{\Omega}d_{uj_{u}^{\Omega}}>0\right].
``` |  | (14) |

For the eligible set
$`\mathcal{E}_{\Omega}=\{u\in\mathcal{U}:g_{uj_{u}^{\Omega}}^{\Omega}\neq 0\}`$,
the agreement rate is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D_{\Omega}=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{E}_{\Omega}|}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{E}_{\Omega}}c_{u}^{\Omega}.
``` |  | (15) |

Thus, $`D_{\Omega}`$ measures how often subsequent training without
Atoms changes action support in the same direction as the explicit Atom
guidance.

#### Aggregation and Results

We aggregate both metrics at the action level within each model scale,
training stage, and task-matching group, such that each recorded action
contributes one observation regardless of token length.
Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Metric 1: Maximum-Token Support Change ‣ Appendix C Procedural Atom Internalization and Composition Analysis ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
reports the aggregated results. Maximum-token support increases across
all eight groups, indicating that the selected action tokens receive
stronger policy support after training. Guidance-direction agreement is
also consistently observed, reaching $`75.0\%`$ for composed Atom
guidance in Early 4B cross-task analysis and $`70.5\%`$ in Late 9B
cross-task analysis. These results provide evidence that both individual
and composed Atom guidance is reflected in subsequent unguided policy
changes, including across different tasks.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  Procedural Pattern |  Core Dependency |  Representative Case |
|  Observation-Conditioned Branching |  A downstream action depends on newly observed information. |  ScienceWorld: AtomSD measures a substance at $`-31\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}`$ and selects the destination specified for temperatures below $`50\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}`$, completing the task. |
|  Constraint-Driven Revision |  An earlier choice must be revised after detecting a violated constraint. |  WebShop: AtomSD rejects an over-budget product, returns to search, and selects a cheaper item satisfying the requested attributes. |
|  Subgoal-State Dependency |  A later subgoal requires the state produced by an earlier operation. |  ALFWorld: AtomSD acquires a potato, heats it, and only then places the heated object in the target receptacle. |
|  Feedback-Guided API Recovery |  Uninformative API responses require adapting the query strategy based on returned feedback. |  StableToolBench: After an empty response, AtomSD revises its pagination strategy, verifies the returned results, and reports nine products grounded in the API output. |

Table 6: Representative cases of recurring procedural patterns observed
in evaluation trajectories.

## Appendix D Qualitative Case Studies

### D.1 Procedural Dependency Patterns

Across evaluation trajectories, we observe several recurring forms of
procedural dependency that distinguish successful agent behavior beyond
simply executing plausible action sequences. We highlight four
representative patterns: (1) *observation-conditioned branching*, (2)
*constraint-driven revision*, (3) *subgoal-state dependency*, and (4)
*feedback-guided API recovery*.
Table [6](#A3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Aggregation and Results ‣ Appendix C Procedural Atom Internalization and Composition Analysis ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
summarizes one representative case for each pattern, followed by
detailed trajectory-level analysis.

#### Observation-Conditioned Branching

This pattern arises when the appropriate downstream action depends on
information revealed only through an intermediate observation. In
ScienceWorld task use-thermometer/384, the agent must first measure an
unknown substance and then select its destination according to the
observed temperature. AtomSD measures $`-31\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}`$ and
subsequently places the substance in the box designated for temperatures
below $`50\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}`$, successfully completing the task. In
contrast, unsuccessful baseline trajectories exhibit errors such as
incorrect thermometer use, repeated invalid actions, and interactions
with unrelated objects, failing to obtain the measurement needed for the
subsequent placement decision. This case illustrates that procedural
competence requires not only acquiring relevant information, but also
conditioning subsequent actions on the observed outcome.

#### Constraint-Driven Revision

This pattern captures situations in which an initially plausible choice
must be revised after newly observed information reveals a constraint
violation. In WebShop task 1451, the requested sweater must satisfy
multiple constraints, including color, size, fit, and a price below
\$40. AtomSD first inspects a \$100 candidate, recognizes the price
mismatch, returns to search, and selects a cheaper product before
configuring the requested color and size, obtaining a score of 100. By
comparison, failed baseline trajectories exhibit incomplete constraint
satisfaction, such as purchasing after selecting the color without
configuring the requested size. The case highlights the ability to
revise an intermediate decision rather than persist with a candidate
that no longer satisfies the task constraints.

#### Subgoal-State Dependency

This pattern occurs when a later subgoal depends on a state established
by an earlier operation. In an ALFWorld heat-and-place task, the potato
must be heated before it can satisfy the final placement goal. AtomSD
first acquires the potato, executes heat potato 1 with microwave 1,
observes confirmation of the state change, and then places the heated
potato in the garbage can, completing the task in eight steps.
Meanwhile, failed baseline trajectories include irrelevant object
manipulations that divert execution from the required acquire–heat–place
sequence. This case illustrates the need to preserve state dependencies
across subgoals, ensuring that the output of one procedure satisfies the
requirements of the next.

#### Feedback-Guided API Recovery

This pattern arises when an API response is uninformative or
inconsistent, requiring the agent to revise its query strategy based on
returned feedback. In StableToolBench task G1_instruction/32617, the
user asks for all products in the Clothing category and their total
count. AtomSD initially receives an empty result, then inspects the
available categories and adjusts its requests until it retrieves nine
valid products together with a reported count of nine. It subsequently
verifies the result through additional pagination checks and grounds its
final answer in the returned API data. Unsuccessful baseline
trajectories instead exhibit continued querying despite obtaining
nonempty results, without consolidating the retrieved information into a
final answer. This case illustrates feedback-guided recovery: when an
initial tool call is uninformative, the agent uses subsequent
observations to revise its interaction strategy and recover a grounded
answer.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  Intent |  When |  Do |  Avoid |
|  Collect ingredients |  Required ingredients have been identified from the recipe. |  Move each required ingredient into a suitable common container. |  Leaving ingredients outside the container or mixing prematurely. |
|  Mix the contents |  All required ingredients are in one accessible, stable container, and the recipe calls for mixing. |  Mix the container and observe whether the target substance is produced. |  Mixing incomplete or separated ingredients, or ignoring mixing errors. |
|  Acknowledge the product |  The desired substance has been created and its location is known. |  Focus on the created substance and confirm task completion. |  Focusing on the wrong object or continuing without acknowledging the goal. |

Table 7: Paraphrases of Procedural Atoms extracted from successful
training trajectories.

|           |       |            |
|-----------|-------|------------|
| Method    | Score | Outcome    |
| GRPO      | 33    | Incomplete |
| OPSD      | 25    | Incomplete |
| GRPO+OPSD | 33    | Incomplete |
| SDPO      | 8     | Incomplete |
| Skill-SD  | 33    | Incomplete |
| SDAR      | 33    | Incomplete |
| AtomSD    | 100   | Complete   |

Table 8: Episode-level comparison on the dough task.

### D.2 Composition of Internalized Atoms

We use a ScienceWorld chemistry case to illustrate how Procedural Atoms
acquired during training can be reflected in the final model’s behavior.
The task requires the agent to *make dough from flour and water and then
focus on the resulting product*. During evaluation, the model receives
only the task itself, without any Atoms or teacher guidance.

#### Atoms Learned During Training

From earlier successful training trajectories, AtomSD extracts three
relevant Atoms: (1) place the required ingredients into the same
container, (2) mix them only after all ingredients are ready, and (3)
focus on the target product after it has been created.
Table [7](#A4.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Feedback-Guided API Recovery ‣ D.1 Procedural Dependency Patterns ‣ Appendix D Qualitative Case Studies ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents")
summarizes the corresponding Atoms. These Atoms are extracted from
different successful training tasks, yet capture complementary
procedures that can be reused and composed to solve new task instances.

#### Internalization and Composition

In the evaluation task, AtomSD follows the same procedural structure. It
places water and flour into the same glass cup, mixes them to produce
dough, and then focuses on the dough to complete the task. The
reappearance of these procedures without explicit Atom guidance suggests
that the learned procedural knowledge has been internalized by the
model, while their sequential use illustrates how multiple Atoms can be
composed to solve a new interaction. As shown in
Table [8](#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Feedback-Guided API Recovery ‣ D.1 Procedural Dependency Patterns ‣ Appendix D Qualitative Case Studies ‣ AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents"),
AtomSD completes the task with a score of 100, whereas all compared
baselines fail to complete it.
````
